To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have isolated a mutant DapA allele of soybean that encodes a DS enzyme that is insensitive to inhibition by lysine.

three mutations in the soybean DAP A gene, encoding dihydrodipolicinate synthase, resulted in an enzyme that is insensitive to feedback inhibition by lysine, and that this enzyme was able to catalyze the first reaction in the lysine biosynthetic pathway in transgenic tobacco plants.

we cloned the DapA (encoding the dihydrodipiolinate synthase) gene of soybean, expressed the gene in Escherchia coli to obtain the enzyme, and then created mutations in the DapA genes that resulted in an enzyme that was insensitive to lysine inhibition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the isolation and characterization of a mutant of a lysine-sensitive enzyme that is insensitive to lysine inhibition.

the cloning and expression of a soybean dihydrodiplicolinate synthase gene in Eschericha coli, and the construction of mutant forms of the gene which encode enzymes with lysine-insensitive DS activity.
the identification of mutations that alter lysine sensitivity in soybean DapB and DapA genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the soybean DAP-A gene encodes an enzyme that is sensitive to feedback inhibition.
the three mutations in the soybean DAP A gene, when expressed in E. colt, result in lysine-insensitive DS activities.
the soybean DAPA gene has been successfully mutated to produce a lysine-insensitive enzyme.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have cloned the DapA cDNA and expressed the protein in E. coli.

we have successfully mutated the DapA genes of both soybean and Arabidopsis thaliana to create lysine-insensitive DS enzymes, which will allow us to investigate the effects of elevated lysine levels in transgenic plants.
we have identified two amino acid residues in the soybean DAPA gene that are responsible for lysine feedback inhibition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to generate a lysine-insensitive form of DS in plants.
the lysine-insensitive DS activities encoded by the soybean mutants were able to support the growth of E. coli in the presence of 1 mM exogenous lysine.
we were able to create mutations in the DapA protein that made the protein insensitive to lysine inhibition.
